questions.question: Discuss the mechanism through which the interest rate ensures that any leakage from the income stream (savings) is returned as investment. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss the mechanism through which the interest rate ensures th at any leakage from the
  • income stream (savings) is returned as investment.
  • According to Classical economists, the interest rate acts as an automatic equilibrating mechanism
  • between savings and investment. When households save, they withdraw money from the income
  • stream, creating a leakage. This increased supply of loanable funds drives the interest rate downward,
  • which in turn makes borrowing cheaper for firms. Encouraged by lower borrowing costs,
  • entrepreneurs increase investment, thereby re -injecting the leaked savings back into the income
  • stream. Classical economists thus believed that through this flexible interest rate mechanism, savings
  • and investment are always brought into equality without any need for government intervention.
  • • 1 mark — Identifying savings as leakage and interest rate as the equilibrating mechanism
  • • 1 mark — Explaining how lower interest rates encourage investment
  • • 1 mark — Concluding that savings and investment are brought to equality automatically

questions.question: Explain the role of aggregate demand in determining employment according to Keynes. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the role of aggregate demand in determining employment according to Keynes.
  • Keynes fundamentally rejected the Classical notion that supply creates its own demand (Say's Law).
  • He argued that the level of employment in an economy is determined by the level of effective demand,
  • AD = C + I) Entrepreneurs decide how much to produce and how many workers to employ based on
  • their expectations of aggregate demand. If aggregate demand is insufficient, output contracts and
  • involuntary unemployment emerges. Keynes concluded that full employment is not automatic but can
  • only be achieved when aggregate demand is raised to an adequate level, which may require deliberate
  • government intervention.
  • • 1 mark — Rejecting Say's Law and introducing effective demand (AD = C + I)
  • • 1 mark — Explaining how insufficient AD leads to involuntary unemployment
  • • 1 mark — Concluding that full employment requires deliberate raising of aggregate demand

questions.question: How does Fisher explain the relationship between money supply and price level? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• How does Fisher explain the relationship between money supply and price level?
  • Irving Fisher explained this relationship through his famous Equation of Exchange: MV = PT ,
  • where M is the money supply, V is the velocity of circulation, P is the price level, and T is the volume
  • of transactions. Fisher assumed that V and T remain constant in the short run. Under these
  • assumptions, any increase in the money supply leads to a direct and proportional increase in the price
  • level. Doubling M will double P. Money is therefore considered neutral — it affects only nominal
  • variables like prices and not real variables like output or employment.
  • • 1 mark — Stating the equation MV = PT with explanation of terms
  • • 1 mark — Explaining the assumptions of constant V and T
  • • 1 mark — Concluding that money supply and price level are directly and proportionally related

questions.question: Define the concept of effective demand in Keynesian economics. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Define the concept of effective demand in Keynesian economics
  • This concept is central to the entire Keynesian system. Effective demand refers to the level of
  • aggregate demand at which the economy reaches equilibrium, that is, where aggregate supply equals
  • aggregate demand. It represents the point at which entrepreneurs' expected revenues match their costs
  • of production, and it is this expectation that determines how much output they will produce and how
  • many workers they will employ. A deficiency of effective demand results in unemployment, while
  • excess demand leads to inflation.
  • • 1 mark — Defining effective demand as the equilibrium point of AS and AD
  • • 1 mark — Explaining that it determines output and employment decisions of entrepreneurs
  • • 1 mark — Stating that deficiency leads to unemployment and excess leads to inflation

questions.question: What is meant by Permanent Income? / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• What is meant by Permanent Income?
  • The concept of Permanent Income was introduced by Milton Friedman as the foundation of his
  • Permanent Income Hypothesis. Permanent income refers to the expected long -run average income
  • that an individual anticipates receiving steadil y over their lifetime, based on their assets, skills, and
  • earning capacity. Friedman distinguished this from transitory income, which represents unexpected
  • or temporary gains and losses. He argued that people base their consumption decisions on permanent
  • income rather than current income, smoothing out their spending over time. A temporary windfall,
  • being transitory, would largely be saved rather than consumed, as it does not alter the individual's
  • perception of their long-run income level.
  • • 1 mark — Defining permanent income as expected long-run average income
  • • 1 mark — Distinguishing it from transitory income
  • • 1 mark — Explaining that consumption is based on permanent income, not current income

questions.question: How does stagflation differ from regular inflation? / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• How does stagflation differ from regular inflation?
  • Regular inflation refers to a sustained rise in the general price level, typically associated with rising
  • output and low unemployment, often caused by excess demand in the economy. Stagflation is a
  • situation where high inflation coexists with economic stag nation and rising unemployment.
  • Stagflation is generally caused by supply-side shocks, as seen during the 1970s oil crisis, rather than
  • excess demand, which is why conventional demand management tools prove inadequate.
  • • 1 mark — Defining regular inflation with its causes and characteristics
  • • 1 mark — Defining stagflation and its coexistence of inflation and unemployment
  • • 1 mark — Explaining the difference in causes and why conventional policy tools fail

questions.question: Compare Ricardian Equivalence with the Keynesian view on fiscal multipliers. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Compare Ricardian Equivalence with the Keynesian view on fiscal multipliers.
  • The Keynesian view holds that an increase in government spending raises aggregate demand directly,
  • and through the multiplier effect, and increases income and employment. The fiscal policy is very
  • effective and the fiscal multiplier is greater than one.
  • But Ricardian Equivalence, associated with Robert Barro building on Ricardo, challenges this view
  • entirely. It argues that rational, forward -looking consumers, upon observing a rise in government
  • borrowing, anticipate higher taxes in the future to repay the debt. They therefore increase their savings
  • today to prepare for that future burden, fully offsetting the government's interventions. The result is
  • a fiscal multiplier of zero, rendering fiscal policy ineffective.
  • • 1 mark — Explaining the Keynesian view with multiplier greater than one
  • • 1 mark — Explaining Ricardian Equivalence and the anticipation of future taxes
  • • 1 mark — Contrasting the two — multiplier greater than one versus multiplier of zero

questions.question: Distinguish between open inflation and suppressed inflation. / [CO4] [3x10 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Distinguish between open inflation and suppressed inflation.
  • Open inflation refers to a situation where the general price level rises freely and visibly as a result of
  • excess demand over supply, without any government interference. Prices are allowed to adjust
  • upward through normal market forces, making the inflation observable and measurable.
  • Suppressed inflation, also called repr essed inflation, occurs when inflationary pressure exists in the
  • economy but is held back artificially through government controls such as price ceilings, rationing,
  • and subsidies. While prices appear stable on the surface, the underlying imbalance between demand
  • and supply persists.
  • • 1 mark — Defining open inflation with its key characteristic of freely rising prices
  • • 1 mark — Defining suppressed inflation and the role of government controls.

questions.question: What mechanism restores equilibrium if the supply of labor exceeds the demand? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• What mechanism restores equilibrium if the supply of labor exceeds the demand?
  • Classical economists believed the labor market can fix itself without any outside help — if there are
  • more workers looking for jobs than there are jobs available, competition among workers will naturally
  • push wages down. This is the market's built -in correction mechanism . e mployers will hire more
  • workers. At the same time, some workers who feel the lower wage is simply not worth their time will
  • leave the market . So demand for labor goes up while supply comes down — and the gap between
  • them gradually closes until the market finds a new balance. At this new equilibrium, everyone who
  • genuinely wants to work at the going wage has a job. If some people remain unemployed, Classical
  • economists called it voluntary unemployment.
  • • 2 marks — Explaining that excess labour supply pushes wages down through competition among
  • workers
  • • 2 marks — Explaining the dual adjustment — employers hire more as labour becomes cheaper, and
  • some workers voluntarily exit the market
  • • 2 marks — Concluding that the market reaches a new equilibrium and any remaining unemployment
  • is voluntary

• Government intervention makes the Keynesian model more realistic - Examine this
  • statement with reference to the three-sector model.
  • The simple Keynesian model includes only households and firms, making it an incomplete picture
  • of modern economies. The three-sector model corrects this by introducing government spending
  • (G) as an injection and taxation (T) as a leakage, with the new equilibrium condition Y = C + I + G
  • and leakages-injections balance S + T = I + G. This makes the model far more useful. It explains
  • how government spending raises income through the multiplier, how taxation cools excess demand,
  • and how even a balanced budget produces a net increase in income through the balanced budget
  • multiplier. It explains the government's stabilising role. Thus, with government Keynesian model
  • becomes a practical tool for managing real economies.

questions.question: Evaluate the difference between Short run and Long run consumption function with the help of diagrams. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Evaluate the difference between Short run and Long run consumption function with the help
  • of diagrams.
  • The short-run consumption function, based on Keynes, shows consumption as C = a + bY , where
  • there is positive autonomous consumption and the curve starts above the origin with a declining APC.
  • In contrast, the long -run consumption function, supported by Kuznets and later theories, is
  • proportional and passes through the origin, indicating constant APC. In the short run, consumption
  • depends mainly on current income, while in the long run it reflects broader factors like permanent or
  • lifetime income. Graphically, the short -run curve is upward sloping with an intercept, whereas the
  • long-run curve is a straight line from the origin. Thus, the key difference lies in the presence of
  • autonomous consumption and the stability of consumption behaviour over time. (Credit should be
  • given to explanation with diagram)
  • • 2 marks — Explaining the short run consumption function

questions.question: Examine the role of Fiscal policy during inflation. / [CO4] [6x5 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Examine the role of Fiscal policy during inflation.
  • Inflation is essentially a situation where too much money chases too few goods. Fiscal policy tackles
  • this problem by withdrawing excess purchasing power from the economy. The most direct method is
  • cutting government expenditure, which reduces aggregate demand and relieves the upward pressure
  • on prices. Alongside this, raising taxes leaves households and firms with lesser money in hand,
  • thereby squeezing demand further. When the government collects more than it spends, it withdraws
  • purchasing power from the economy and exercises a dampening effect on prices. The government
  • may also borrow from the public through bonds and securities, which mops up excess liquidity from
  • the system and reduces the funds available for spending , thus helping to keep inflationary pressures
  • in check.
  • • 2 marks — Explaining how cutting government expenditure directly reduces aggregate demand
  • • 2 marks — Explaining how raising taxes reduces disposable income and squeezes demand,
  • • 2 marks — Explaining how government borrowing through bonds and securities clears excess
  • liquidity and concluding that contractionary fiscal policy is an effective instrument for price stability
